title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarking Suite, Runbooks & Known Issues
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary:
This page consolidates the serving runtime documentation: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling and instrumentation playbook, benchmarking suite design, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki guidance. Intended audience: runtime engineers, SREs, performance engineers, and any engineer onboarding to serving-runtime work.

1) Overview and Objectives
- Purpose: Provide a single reference for how Redwood's GPU-optimized serving runtime is designed, how kernels are scheduled, how we profile and benchmark, and how to operate and triage incidents.
- Goals: predictable tail latency, high throughput, efficient GPU utilization, graceful degradation, reproducible benchmarks, and clear operational runbooks.
- Key SLOs (service-wide):
  - P50 latency (1 request, 512 tokens): <= 30ms
  - P95 latency (1 request, 512 tokens): <= 120ms
  - Token-throughput per-GPU (steady-state): documented per-model in model-catalog (see section 4)
  - Availability: 99.95% (Dedicated), 99.9% (Hosted)

2) Runtime architecture (high level)
- Components:
  - Frontend API gateway (route selection, auth, throttling)
  - Router / policy engine (smart routing: latency, cost, region, model-compatibility)
  - Scheduler / dispatcher (request coalescing, batch assembly)
  - Worker runtime (per-GPU process with kernel executor, KV cache, tokenizer service)
  - Caching layer (prefix and KV cache with eviction policy)
  - Observability pipeline (traces, structured spans, token-level metrics)
- Data flow (simplified): API -> Router -> Scheduler (batch assembly) -> Worker runtime -> Kernel executor -> Postprocessor -> Response
- Design notes:
  - Worker runtime isolates model memory per-process to simplify eviction and heap safe-points.
  - Continuous batching: scheduler maintains per-model batchers with adaptive batch size bounded by latency SLOs.
  - KV cache affinity: requests with hot prefixes are routed to workers with warm KV caches when possible.

3) Kernel scheduling strategy
- Goals: maximize arithmetic intensity, minimize kernel-launch overhead, and preserve latency SLOs.
- Layers of scheduling:
  1. Operator fusion & chosen kernels: runtime consults kernel registry (CPU/GPU) based on model op pattern and quantization profile.
  2. Micro-batching: for attention and dense kernels we prefer fused-kernel micro-batches (N tokens) to amortize kernel launch cost.
  3. Stream management: use dedicated CUDA streams per-request group; priority streams for single-request low-latency paths.
  4. Preemptible cooperative scheduling: long-running conversational generation tasks yield periodically to low-latency requests using GPU stream priorities and small-kernel preemption points.
- Tuning knobs (configurable):
  - max_batch_size (per-model)
  - batch_timeout_ms (adaptive)
  - micro_batch_tokens
  - kernel_selection_policy (latency|throughput|balanced)
  - stream_priority_threshold
- Example kernel-selection table (excerpt):
  | Model class | Sequence length | Preferred kernel | Quantized variants |
  |-------------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------|
  | 7B decoder | <= 1024 | fused-attn-epilog | 8-bit O1, 4-bit O2 |
  | 13B decoder | <= 2048 | block-sparse-attn | 8-bit O1 |
  | Large chat | >2048 | chunked-kv + streaming | quantized + cache |

4) Profiling & instrumentation playbook
- Objective: reproducible collection of CPU/GPU metrics, kernel timelines, and request-level traces to find bottlenecks.
- Required tooling: nsight-systems (subset traces), CUPTI metrics, perf (host), eBPF (sched events), custom token-level tracing (our tracer).
- Data to collect for a targeted incident or regression test:
  1. Full request trace (trace id) with spans: router -> scheduler -> batcher -> worker -> kernel executor.
  2. GPU timeline (nsight-systems capture, 2s window around incident) with kernel durations and stream contention.
  3. CUPTI counters: SM utilization, achieved occupancy, L2 hit rate, DRAM throughput.
  4. CPU-side: process-level CPU, memcpy time, serialization time.
  5. Scheduler logs: batch sizes, batch assembly latency, dropped/badly packed batches.
- Profiling procedure (step-by-step):
  1. Identify affected trace ids (from observability dashboards).
  2. Capture a 10s nsight-systems snapshot on the affected worker (nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx -o /tmp/trace).
  3. Export CUPTI counters for the same interval (counters configured per GPU type).
  4. Run host perf for syscall/memcpy hotspots.
  5. Correlate with scheduler logs and batcher metrics.
  6. Annotate findings in a profiling ticket and link to traces.
- Common fingerprints and what they indicate:
  - Large number of 1-item batches -> scheduler misconfigured or traffic skew; check front-end routing and batching thresholds.
  - High memcpy + low SM utilization -> poor data packing, CPU-side serialization, or tokenization bottleneck.
  - Long tail of small kernels -> too many kernel launches; adjust micro_batch_tokens or enable fused kernels.
  - High L2 miss / DRAM throughput -> model weights not in L2 / memory thrashing; consider pinning model to fewer processes or adjust cache eviction.

5) Benchmarking suite (design & how-to)
- Purpose: produce reproducible throughput/latency profiles across model variants, quantization levels, and sequence length distributions.
- Suite components:
  - Workload generator (wg-runner) with YAML profiles (concurrency, arrival process, token distribution).
  - Reference datasets: prompt-sets (chat, completion, embeddings) and synthetic-long sequences.
  - Harness: automated provisioning scripts to spin test pools, deploy model artifacts, and run load phases.
  - Analysis tools: Jupyter notebooks and scripts to compute P50/P95/P99, gpu-token/s, cost-per-token.
- Benchmark procedure (recommended):
  1. Choose model + quantization profile + hardware SKU.
  2. Provision a dedicated test pool (3 identical GPUs recommended).
  3. Warm caches with 10k promotional requests (simulate production prefixes).
  4. Run baseline ramp (5m) -> steady-state (10m) -> stress (2x expected qps for 5m).
  5. Collect traces and metrics; run nsight snapshot during stress window.
  6. Compare against golden baseline CSV and publish results.
- Key metrics reported:
  - tokens/sec per GPU, avg tokens per request, cost-per-1M-tokens estimate, P95 latency for various sequence lengths, batch size distribution.
- CI integration: benchmarks run nightly on a representative GPU fleet; regressions (>5% throughput or >10% P95 latency) open an alerting issue.

6) Release notes (recent highlights)
- v2026.12.20 (stable):
  - Kernel selection policy enhanced to prefer fused kernels for small sequence lengths; median P95 improved by 18% on 7B models.
  - Adaptive batch_timeout_ms now uses EWMA of arrival intervals; reduces small-batch tail events.
  - New CUPTI-based health export added to observability pipeline.
- v2027.01.05 (hotfix):
  - Fixed incorrect stream priority handling that caused starvation of low-latency requests under heavy generation workloads.
  - Improved model pinning heuristics to reduce KV cache churn.

7) Known issues (operational)
- Issue #1023: Intermittent high memcpy times on p4d nodes when multiple model sizes run concurrently. Workaround: co-locate only homogeneous model families or set limit_per_gpu_models=1. Status: investigating, assigned to Diego.
- Issue #1147: Rare CUDA driver timeout after long-running heavy sampling. Workaround: configure shorter generation chunks or enable periodic checkpoint/yield. Status: mitigated in v2027.01.05.
- Issue #1219: Scheduler metrics occasionally show negative batch assembly latency due to clock skew between hosts. Workaround: ensure NTP/PTP sync; scheduled fix: use monotonic timestamps in logs.

8) Runtime runbooks (critical operational procedures)
- Runbook: High tail latency for a specific model
  1. Identify impacted endpoints and trace ids from the dashboard.
  2. Check per-model batch size distribution (Grafana: batcher.model.<model>.distribution).
  3. If high fraction of single-item batches: temporarily set max_batch_size to a lower value and reduce batch_timeout_ms to force faster dispatch, or enable low-latency policy.
  4. Capture nsight & CUPTI traces for sample worker; run profiling playbook.
  5. If memcpy is the bottleneck, route traffic to warmed workers or increase worker CPU allocation for serialization threads.
  6. Open postmortem if incident >30m or customer impact.
- Runbook: Worker GPU OOMs on deployment upgrade
  1. Inspect model artifact sizes and quantization.
  2. Check runtime flags: enable memory-saver-mode, reduce pipeline parallelism, or deploy with reduced num_workers_per_gpu.
  3. Rollback to previous model artifact if needed and notify release manager.
- Runbook: Degraded throughput during stress tests
  1. Validate scheduling policy (throughput vs latency).
  2. Confirm kernel selection: if fallback to suboptimal kernels occurred, re-run benchmark with kernel logs enabled.
  3. Scale out worker pool temporarily and re-run stress window.

9) Team wiki & ownership
- Owners: runtime-architecture (Asha Patel), kernel-scheduling (Diego Fernandez), profiling & benchmarks (Li Wei), runtime-sre (Maya Thompson).
- Team wiki pointers:
  - Quickstart: how to run a local worker and attach profiler: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/quickstart-run-local-worker
  - Benchmark dashboards: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-dashboards
  - Kernel registry docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-registry
- Onboarding checklist for new runtime engineers (summary):
  1. Read this consolidated page.
  2. Run the wg-runner with the small-profile locally.
  3. Complete the profiling lab (Nsight + CUPTI) and submit results.
  4. Shadow an oncall rotation.

10) Appendix: common CLI snippets and config examples
- Start nsight capture (example):
  sudo nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --capture-range=nvtx --output=/tmp/serve-trace && gzip /tmp/serve-trace.qdrep
- Example wg-runner YAML (minimal):
  workload: chat-small
  concurrency: 50
  arrival: poisson
  sequence_length_distribution: [64, 128, 256]
- Example runtime config fragment (toml-like):
  [model_defaults]
  max_batch_size = 64
  batch_timeout_ms = 12
  micro_batch_tokens = 32
  kernel_selection_policy = "balanced"

If you find inaccuracies or missing procedures, please file a doc-edit PR against this page and tag owners. For urgent incidents, alert runtime-sre via PagerDuty.
